'''Joan Feigenbaum''' (born 1958 in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York City|New York]]) is a [[computer scientist]] with a background in [[mathematics]]. She is the [[Grace Murray Hopper]] Professor of [[Computer science|Computer Science]] at [[Yale University]]<ref name="gmhp">{{citation|title=Joan Feigenbaum Named the Grace Murray Hopper Professor|url=https://news.yale.edu/2008/07/18/joan-feigenbaum-named-grace-murray-hopper-professor|date=July 18, 2008|journal=Yale News}}</ref> and an Amazon Scholar in the [[AWS]] Cryptography group. At Yale, she also holds a secondary appointment in the Department of [[Economics]]. She has worked in several research areas over the course of her career, including cryptography, security, and privacy; computational complexity; algorithmic mechanism design; massive-data-stream algorithmics; and, most recently, computer science and law.

==Education and career==
Feigenbaum did her undergraduate work in Mathematics at [[Harvard University]].  She became interested in computers during the Summer Research Program at [[Bell Labs]] between her junior and senior years.  She then earned a Ph.D. in [[computer science]] at [[Stanford University]], under the supervision of [[Andrew Yao]],<ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=Joan Feigenbaum|id=69410}}</ref> while working summers at [[Bell Labs]].  Upon finishing her PhD in 1986, she joined [[AT&T Bell Labs]]. She moved to Yale in 2000, became the Hopper Professor at Yale in 2008,<ref name="gmhp"/> and became an Amazon Scholar in 2018.

==Family==
She is married to Jeffrey Nussbaum.  They have a son, Sam Baum. Baum was chosen as the child's surname, because it is the [[Longest common substring problem|greatest common suffix]] of Feigenbaum and Nussbaum.<ref>''Notable Women in Mathematics, a Biographical Dictionary'', edited by Charlene Morrow and Teri Perl, Greenwood Press, 1998. p 50.</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 1998, Feigenbaum was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Berlin<ref>{{cite book|author=Feigenbaum, Joan|chapter=Games, complexity classes, and approximation algorithms|title=Doc. Math. (Bielefeld) Extra Vol. ICM Berlin, 1998, vol. III|year=1998|pages=429–439|chapter-url=https://www.elibm.org/ft/10011599000}}</ref> and, in 1999, she was a Plenary Speaker at the [[American Mathematical Society]] Winter Meeting in San Antonio.<ref>{{citation|url=https://jointmathematicsmeetings.org/meetings/national/jmm/2031_invited.html|title=AMS 1999 Winter Meeting's Invited Addresses|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|accessdate=2025-06-23}}</ref> 

In 2001, she was named a fellow of the [[Association for Computing Machinery]] for her "foundational and highly influential contributions to cryptographic complexity theory, authorization and trust management, massive-data-stream computation, and algorithmic mechanism design."<ref>{{citation|url=https://awards.acm.org/award-recipients/feigenbaum_N967745|title=ACM Fellows: Joan Feigenbaum|publisher=[[Association for Computing Machinery]]|accessdate=2025-06-23}}.</ref> In 2012, she was named a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref>{{citation|title=AAAS Members Elected as Fellows|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=338|date=November 30, 2012|pages=1168–1171|doi=10.1126/science.338.6111.1166 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and chosen by the Connecticut Technology Council as a Woman of Innovation. In 2013, she was elected as a member<ref name="Joan Feigenbaum CASE">{{cite web | title=Connecticut Academy of Science & Engineering | website=Member public profile | url=https://casemembers.wildapricot.org/Sys/PublicProfile/8708920 | access-date=2022-11-29}}</ref> of the [[Connecticut Academy of Science and Engineering]]. In 2024, she was named a fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]]<ref>{{citation|url=https://services27.ieee.org/fellowsdirectory/getdetailprofile.html?custNum=rTGHMcnDbkkQZeCdD%2F8jqA%3D%3D&bccaptions=Alphabetical%20Listing%20&bclocations=%2Ffellowsdirectory%2Fhome.html|title=IEEE Fellows Directory: Joan Feigenbaum|publisher=[[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]]|accessdate=2025-06-23}}</ref> and a fellow of the [[International Association for Cryptologic Research]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.iacr.org/fellows/|title=IACR Fellows|publisher=[[International Association for Cryptologic Research]]|accessdate=2025-06-23}}.</ref> In May 2020, she won the Test-of-Time Award<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.ieee-security.org/TC/SP2020/awards.html|title=2020 Awards|publisher= IEEE Computer Society Technical Committee on Security and Privacy in cooperation with the International Association for Cryptologic Research|accessdate=2025-06-23}}</ref> from the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy for her 1996 paper (with [[Matt Blaze]] and Jack Lacy) entitled "Decentralized Trust Management."

Professor Feigenbaum has served the computing community in many roles over the course of her career.  Currently, she serves as an Editorial-Board Member for the [[Communications of the ACM]]<ref>{{citation|url=https://cacm.acm.org/editorial-staff-board/|title=CACM Editorial Board and Staff|publisher=[[Association for Computing Machinery]]|accessdate=2025-06-23}}</ref> and a Steering-Committee Member for the ACM Symposium on Computer Science and Law.<ref>{{citation|url=https://computersciencelaw.org/organizers/steeringcmte/|title=ACM CS&Law Steering Committee|accessdate=2025-06-23}}</ref>
